top_cited_works.title: Experimental investigation of Rayleigh–Taylor mixing at small Atwood numbers
top_cited_works.abstract: The self-similar evolution to turbulence of a multi-mode Rayleigh–Taylor mix at small density differences ( $A_{t} \sim 7.5 \times 10^{ - 4}$ ), is investigated through particle image velocimetry (PIV), and high-resolution thermocouple measurements. The density difference has been achieved through a temperature difference in the fluid. Cold fluid enters above the hot in a closed channel to form an unstable interface. This buoyancy-driven mixing experiment allows for long data collection times, short transients, and is statistically steady. First-, second-, and third-order statistics with spectra of velocity and temperature fields are presented. Analysis of the measurements has shed light on the structure of mixing as it develops to a self-similar regime in this flow. The onset of self-similarity is marked by the development of a self-preserving form of the temperature spectra, and the collapse of velocity profiles expressed in self-similar units. Vertical velocity fluctuations dominate horizontal velocity fluctuations in this experiment, with a ratio approaching 2:1 in the self-similar regime. top_cited_works.title: Rayleigh–Taylor and Richtmyer–Meshkov instabilities: A journey through scales
top_cited_works.abstract: Hydrodynamic instabilities such as Rayleigh–Taylor (RT) and Richtmyer–Meshkov (RM) instabilities usually appear in conjunction with the Kelvin–Helmholtz (KH) instability and are found in many natural phenomena and engineering applications . They frequently result in turbulent mixing, which has a major impact on the overall flow development and other effective material properties. This can either be a desired outcome, an unwelcome side effect, or just an unavoidable consequence, but must in all cases be characterized in any model. The RT instability occurs at an interface between different fluids, when the light fluid is accelerated into the heavy. The RM instability may be considered a special case of the RT instability, when the acceleration provided is impulsive in nature such as that resulting from a shock wave. In this pedagogical review, we provide an extensive survey of the applications and examples where such instabilities play a central role. top_cited_works.title: A comparative study of the turbulent Rayleigh–Taylor instability using high-resolution three-dimensional numerical simulations: The Alpha-Group collaboration
top_cited_works.abstract: The turbulent Rayleigh–Taylor instability is investigated in the limit of strong mode-coupling using a variety of high-resolution, multimode, three dimensional numerical simulations (NS). The perturbations are initialized with only short wavelength modes so that the self-similar evolution (i.e., bubble diameter Db∝amplitude hb) occurs solely by the nonlinear coupling (merger) of saturated modes. After an initial transient, it is found that hb∼αbAgt2, where A=Atwood number, g=acceleration, and t=time. The NS yield Db∼hb/3 in agreement with experiment but the simulation value αb∼0.025±0.003 is smaller than the experimental value αb∼0.057±0.008. By analyzing the dominant bubbles, it is found that the small value of αb can be attributed to a density dilution due to fine-scale mixing in our NS without interface reconstruction (IR) or an equivalent entrainment in our NS with IR. This may be characteristic of the mode coupling limit studied here and the associated αb may represent a lower bound that is insensitive to the initial amplitude. Larger values of αb can be obtained in the presence of additional long wavelength perturbations and this may be more characteristic of experiments. ...

recent_works.title: Unsteady Acceleration Droplet Breakup
recent_works.abstract: Understanding droplet breakup is essential for designing hypersonic vehicles that can survive atmospheric droplet impacts. The droplets experience a highly unsteady flow condition in the bow shock of these vehicles as the result of their geometry. While abundant literature exists on droplet breakup, there is a dearth of work considering the effects an unsteady flow has on breakup. This paper examines droplet breakup under unsteady conditions in experiments. A coupled shock-expansion wave system is used to create conditions similar to those found in bow shocks using a shock tube facility. Droplet deformation and breakup morphology are measured using Planar Laser-Induced Fluorescence images at high spatiotemporal resolution. The breakup behavior of these droplets is analyzed and compared to a constant flow, shock-driven case. Droplet deformation is seen to scale with droplet size and Weber number decay during breakup. These initial findings suggest a faster deformation rate under unsteady conditions.

recent_works.title: Numerical Simulations of Liquid-Fueled Rotating Detonation Engines Using the KHRT Droplet Breakup Model
recent_works.abstract: We present results from the numerical investigation of a three-dimensional unrolled Rotating Detonation Engine (RDE) with detailed particle modeling using the Eulerian-Lagrangian method. The simulations were performed with n-dodecane injected in both liquid and vapor phases and pure oxygen as reactants. Mono-disperse injection is considered with three different injection diameters of 5, 15 and 30 µm. Droplet breakup was modeled based on the stability of Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor instability (KHRT) modes that form on the droplet surface. We find that most droplets in the refill region of the RDE did not undergo KH breakup, as they interacted with the detonation wave before the predicted breakup time is reached. On the other hand, RT unstable modes were found to be stabilized by surface tension forces. However, following interaction with the detonation wave, rapid breakup and evaporation is observed at the detonation front. We show that due to the particle lag in the refill region, the upper section of the detonation wave is devoid of liquid fuel. recent_works.title: Hybrid Modeling Approach for Designing Variable Twist Blades: Implementing CFD and Data Driven Models for Ocean Current Turbine Twist Optimization
recent_works.abstract: Abstract The paper below discusses a design approach for Ocean Current Turbines (OCTs) with variable twist blades for improved energy capture and reduced loading. This paper focuses on the intersection of two key methodologies for simulating rotor behavior. The first methodology is the OpenFAST models used to optimize, and the second simulation method is CFD for detailed flow overview. The OpenFAST software developed by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) is used in conjunction with Aerodyne to produce the turbine characteristics at various speeds; this is used for baseline results. The CFD setup uses a virtual disk model with Large Eddy Simulation (LES) to capture the detailed wake dynamics of the flow field. Simulations were employing STAR-CCM+ to capture wake evolution and flow recovery trends, validating the potential benefits of adaptive rotor strategies. This paper also covers a hybrid modeling methodology currently being tested to interface the optimization techniques and CFD models. recent_works.title: Variable Acceleration Shock-Driven Droplet Breakup
recent_works.abstract: At hypersonic velocities, atmospheric droplets pose a significant threat to aircrafts because of their high kinetic energy, which is imparted at impact, causing damage to the vehicle’s thermal protection systems. Before impact, droplets are processed by the vehicle’s bow shock, which is composed of a strong oblique shock and subsequent expansion waves. It is essential to understand how droplets break apart upon interaction with bow shocks to predict their potential to damage the vehicle. Although the majority of research efforts to date have focused on droplet breakup under constant acceleration, droplets interacting with a bow shock experience a more complex and unsteady acceleration history. The effects of droplet breakup under unsteady acceleration are poorly understood. To address this gap in understanding, a new shock tube facility was designed and built to study droplet breakup under a combined shock and expansion wave acceleration. Preliminary experiments show that the deformation and onset of breakup for millimeter-scale droplets under this unsteady acceleration are similar to those of purely shock-driven droplet breakup experiments. recent_works.title: Shock-Induced Deformation and Kinematics of Acetone Droplets
recent_works.abstract: Using detailed 2D axisymmetric numerical simulations, we investigate the deformation and kinematics of a 10 µm acetone droplet impacted by a Mach 2.4 shock wave. The simulations utilize high-fidelity numerical methods to capture the complex interfacial instabilities and subsequent droplet breakup dynamics, focusing on a Weber number of We=565. Results reveal the evolution of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities on the droplet surface and their role in droplet deformation and breakup, characterized by thin ligament formation and shedding. The study also compares the droplet deformation rates obtained from the simulations as well as droplet drag and kinematic quantities with predictions from the original Taylor Analogy Breakup (OTAB) model and a modified TAB (MTAB) model. Discrepancies between the simulation and model predictions at late times highlight the need for further improvements to these models. The findings provide insights into the fundamental physics of droplet deformation under shockwave conditions, which are pertinent for applications in propulsion and combustion systems.
